newsitem.title: USA: All U.S. troops may get anthrax vaccination.
newsitem.headline: All U.S. troops may get anthrax vaccination.

text.p: Defence Secretary William Perry on Wednesday promised a quick decision on a proposal from his military chiefs to inoculate all U.S. troops against deadly anthrax in a possible germ-warfare attack.
Perry told reporters he expected to get the sweeping recommendation from Army Gen. John Shalikashvili, chairman of the military Joint Chiefs of Staff, within a few days.

"When that comes, I will look at it very carefully and make a prompt decision on it," he said in response to questions during a photo opportunity with visiting Italian Defence Minister Beniamino Andreatta.

Air Force Col. Doug Kennett, a Pentagon spokesman, earlier on Wednesday confirmed a Washington Post report that senior U.S. officers favoured the initiative in what would be the Pentagon's first regular inoculation programme for all troops against a germ agent.
Anthrax is an infectious disease of wild and domesticated animals, especially cattle and sheep, which causes profuse bleeding and can be transmitted to people.

Kennett spoke as the Pentagon continued to contend with a growing controversy over the exposure of perhaps tens of thousands of Gulf War veterans to Iraqi chemical agents in the 1991 destruction of an arms bunker in southern Iraq.
Defence officials, who asked not to be identified, said it could cost more than $100 million to immunise 1.5 million military personnel from anthrax.

They confirmed the Post report that Iraq, Russia and as many as 10 other countries have the capability to load spores of anthrax into weapons, although no country is known to have released the bacteria on a battlefield.

The Pentagon, meanwhile, said on Tuesday that at least 15,000 and perhaps far more U.S. Gulf War veterans might have been exposed to chemical weapons in the destruction of an Iraqi ammunition dump five years ago.

Department spokesman Ken Bacon also told reporters that the prestigious private National Academy of Sciences had agreed to a request to study the department's controversial handling of "Gulf War illness."

The Pentagon said two weeks ago that it was notifying 5,000 U.S. troops that they might have been exposed to Sarin nerve gas when chemical rockets and shells were blown up at the Kamisiyah ammunition depot in southern Iraq in March 1991.
"I think we have to think in terms of big numbers. Bigger than 15,000, certainly," Bacon said on Tuesday when pressed by reporters on whether that number could grow significantly.
Published reports suggested in recent weeks that more than 100,000 U.S. troops from several divisions might have been exposed to fallout from a massive white cloud from the explosion.
The issue, in which the Pentagon denied ignoring complaints of veterans or trying to cover up information, has become a major military and political controversy.

The government, on orders from President Bill Clinton, last year mounted a major effort to resolve medical complaints from as many as 60,000 Gulf War veterans. The complaints ranged from numbness to memory loss, but no common cause or so-called Gulf War illness was found .

The Posat reported that the endorsement of the anthrax vaccination plan by top military officials represented a reversal of earlier thinking and reflected heightened Pentagon concern about the prospect of biological attack.
Military leaders initially were dubious about the need for anthrax vaccine, instead favouring work on a multipurpose vaccine that could counter a number of biological warfare agents, the Post said.
